query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In solidified Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloys, the dynamic mechanical behavior is controlled by the rapidly accumulating stacking faults during high-rate or non‐ambient loading. When a critical density of stacking faults is reached, localized deformation mechanisms (such as incipient twinning and/or a partial transformation in the FCC matrix) are activated that boost work hardening and delay shear localization, thereby preserving the strength–ductility balance.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐solidified, homogeneous Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy primarily in a face‐centered cubic (FCC) phase with minimal initial defects.
generation.intervention: Subject identically prepared specimens to uniaxial tensile or compressive tests under controlled strain rates (from quasi‐static to high dynamic) and temperatures (from cryogenic through room temperature to moderately elevated) while performing in situ characterization.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted in a controlled laboratory environment with strain rates spanning from ~10⁻³ s⁻¹ to ~10³ s⁻¹ and temperatures ranging from ~77 K (cryogenic) to ~400 K. All samples should be of identical as‐solidified microstructure without additional secondary phases.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution and accumulation of stacking faults that subsequently trigger localized deformation features such as deformation twins or incipient phase transformation zones.
generation.mechanism: At lower strain rates and ambient temperatures, the alloy deforms mainly by dislocation slip. Under dynamic or non‐ambient conditions, rapid accumulation of stacking faults increases the local defect density. Once a critical threshold is reached, these defects promote local activation of twin formation and/or a subtle transformation from the FCC matrix, which greatly enhances strain hardening and mitigates catastrophic shear localization.
generation.predicted_outcome: Higher strain rates and/or extreme temperatures will correlate with a measurable increase in stacking fault (and, possibly, twin or transformation) density that aligns with improved work hardening and dynamic yield strength. Conversely, under conditions below the critical defect accumulation threshold, the mechanical response will be similar to quasi‐static behavior.
generation.baseline: Mechanical behavior of as‐solidified FeNiCrMn alloy under quasi‐static strain rate at room temperature, where minimal stacking fault accumulation and no significant twinning/transformation are observed.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate in the homogeneous, as‐solidified microstructure; if significant secondary phases or pre‐existing high defect densities are present, or if the loading conditions induce severe adiabatic heating independent of defect accumulation, the mechanism could be masked.
generation.uncertainty: The precise critical stacking fault density and the exact temperature/strain rate thresholds required to trigger the localized deformation mechanisms remain to be quantified. Moreover, whether the local transformation is predominantly twinning or a subtle FCC to HCP (or other) event may require further clarification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of as-solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy specimens. Conduct in situ SEM/TEM mechanical tests under controlled, varying strain rates (from quasi-static to dynamic) and temperatures (from cryogenic to elevated) while mapping the local strain field and defect evolution using digital image correlation (DIC) and high-resolution imaging. Quantitatively correlate the evolution of stacking fault, twin, or phase transformation densities with changes in work hardening and yield strength.
measurements: Stress–strain curves at different strain rates and temperatures
High-resolution imaging (TEM/SEM) for defect (stacking fault, twin) quantification
Phase identification (EBSD/XRD) to detect any localized transformation
Local strain mapping via in situ DIC
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If under dynamic or non-ambient loading conditions no statistically significant increase in stacking fault (or twin/phase transformation) density is observed or if the dynamic yield strength and work-hardening behavior do not correlate with such microstructural changes (i.e., mechanical performance remains unchanged despite variations in defect densities), then the hypothesis is falsified.

In situ micromechanical testing techniques inside scanning electron microscopes (SEMs) are highly utilized tools to study deformation and fracture characteristics of a wide range of materials at scales that were previously unachievable [, ]. Thereby, they provide the possibility to investigate, for example, size effects [], irradiation layers [] or microstructural features [] at their native scale. While indentation based techniques, such as nanoindentation or micropillar compression, are by far the most common methods, tensile testing in such in situ setups has been conducted less frequently, as the experimental effort is considerably higher []. Independent of whether a push-to-pull geometry [] or a gripping geometry [, ] is employed, the sample preparation is more tedious and the time required to conduct an experiment is distinctly longer compared to a single nanoindentation or microcompression test. Therefore, it is desirable to extract as much information as possible from such an individual tensile experiment. Nevertheless, one can envisage the broader scenario shown in schematic fashion in Fig. 4. Specifically, as the deformation energy, and accordingly the defect density, is increased, elastic deformation gives way to the generation of dislocations and their motion, then to deformation twinning, then phase transitions until finally in the extreme high strain (and/or high strain rate) regime, where amorphization can occur. The boundary between each mechanism can be loosely delineated by critical defect densities, which shift the free-energy barrier between different phases. The CrMnFeCoNi HEA has a very low stacking-fault energy, which favors defect accumulation during deformation since low stacking-fault energies lead to the dissociation of dislocations with a larger spacing between the partials; this, in turn, acts to severely inhibit the cross-slip of screw dislocations and consequently reduces the probability of dislocation annihilation.
